name: PHUL

card.summary: A four-day Power Hypertrophy Upper Lower training split that combines heavy strength days with higher-rep size days to build muscle and a more muscular physique.
card.note: Popular programme with little direct published research; the structure is intense and often discussed as intermediate-level.

quick.overview:
PHUL (Power Hypertrophy Upper Lower) is a four-day-a-week weight-training programme that splits the week into two upper-body and two lower-body sessions, one pair of each emphasising heavy strength work and the other emphasising muscle-size volume. For looks, it is a way to add muscle to the shoulders, chest, back, arms and legs, which shapes the physique.

It was written by fitness educator Brandon Campbell and published on Muscle & Strength in 2013, and it spread through YouTube and training apps. There is little published research on PHUL by name; its design resembles upper-lower splits and periodised training studied more broadly.
quick.how: Lifters train upper power, lower power, then (after rest days) upper hypertrophy and lower hypertrophy. Power days use heavy compound lifts in low rep ranges; hypertrophy days use moderate to higher reps and isolation work. Progression is by adding reps and then weight. Results from muscle-building programmes typically build over months.
quick.risks: Risks are those of heavy resistance training: joint and tendon strain, and overtraining if recovery is short. Forum logs describe it as demanding in volume and intensity, and Grokipedia says it is not generally recommended for beginners. People with medical conditions typically consult a clinician first.

lead: PHUL, short for Power Hypertrophy Upper Lower, is a four-day weight-training split created by Brandon Campbell, a fitness educator and YouTuber, and first published on the Muscle & Strength website in February 2013 [1]. It aims to build maximal strength and muscle size in the same week by splitting sessions into power days and hypertrophy days.

For appearance, the programme targets muscle mass across the whole body: each region is trained twice a week, which proponents say is efficient for size and for those with limited schedules [1]. Fitness apps such as Boostcamp and YouTube videos helped spread it [1].
Published research on PHUL itself is not available; commentary on the programme refers to broader work on undulating periodisation and training frequency [1].

chain: Heavy compound lifting on power days
More muscle mass and strength over months
angle.text: PHUL is a structured plan for building muscle, which changes physique: broader shoulders, fuller chest, back, arms and legs. The combined strength and size days are meant to drive both.

infobox: 4 days per week, each region twice [1]

paras: A typical week has upper power on Monday, lower power on Tuesday, rest on Wednesday, upper hypertrophy on Thursday, lower hypertrophy on Friday and rest at the weekend, and the days can be shifted so similar sessions are separated by rest [1].

Power days use roughly 3 to 5 reps on main compound lifts such as bench press, barbell row, squat and deadlift. Hypertrophy days use about 8 to 12 reps, with up to 15 on some lower-body isolation work, with incline presses, flyes, lateral raises, curls, lunges and leg curls [1]. Effort is typically described as leaving one or two reps in reserve, and progression is linear, adding reps within the range and then small weight increases [1].

Proponents say the power and hypertrophy split limits overtraining and supports recovery, and that it fits busy schedules [1]. It is often grouped with PHAT as a powerbuilding programme, with PHUL described as the more compact upper-lower version [1].

Grokipedia notes that the programme lacks extensive peer-reviewed validation and rests mainly on user reports, and that it cites meta-analyses suggesting undulating periodisation can match or outperform linear models when volume is matched [1]. It also says the programme is not generally recommended for beginners because of its intensity and volume, and that deload guidance varies by source [1].
PHUL appears in lifters' training logs on forums such as T Nation, where members describe running upper-lower or power-and-hypertrophy blocks alongside other goals [2].
No studies found. Research exists on related topics, such as training frequency and periodisation, but no published trial tests PHUL by name.

timeline.event: Brandon Campbell publishes PHUL on Muscle & Strength [1].
